accroche: In 1935, an illiterate farmer in the Balkans dictates 12,311 lines from memory, and reopens a debate two thousand years old.
contenu_vulgarise:
On July 12, 1935, in Bijelo Polje, an illiterate farmer named Avdo Međedović finishes dictating a poem of 12,311 lines to two Americans equipped with an aluminum-disc recorder. He began on July 5 and has never written anything down: it is all in his memory, improvised line after line in front of the machine. The two men, Milman Parry and his student Albert Lord, have not come to record folklore for its own sake. They have come to test a hypothesis about Homer.

## The Problem Homer Poses

The Homeric question has stirred philologists since antiquity: who composed the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*? A single man, blind and brilliant, as the legend has it? Several successive authors, gathered under a convenient name? No contemporary document says, and the style poses a further difficulty, the abundance of fixed epithets (“swift-footed Achilles,” “rosy-fingered dawn”) that return without varying, even when they fit the scene poorly. A poet sitting at his table, writing, has little reason to repeat himself this way.

## Parry's Hypothesis

In 1930, in a study published at Harvard, Milman Parry proposes an explanation: these fixed expressions are not a stylistic tic, they are a tool of oral composition. A bard who improvises live, before an audience, with no chance to revise, needs ready-made blocks, fitted to the meter, to keep the rhythm going while he invents what comes next. Parry calls these “formulas.” To test his hypothesis, he needed to observe a living oral tradition. Parry first went to Yugoslavia in the summer of 1933, alone, on a scouting trip. He returned from June 1934 to September 1935, this time with a former student turned assistant, Albert Lord, and a device designed for the expedition, able to record continuously on aluminum discs.

What they find there exceeds their expectations. Singers like Međedović, who never went to school, compose in performance poems of several thousand lines, the length of an *Odyssey*, with no written aid, using the same system of formulas that Parry had spotted in Homer.

## What It Shifts

The conclusion does not identify Homer. It makes the question ill-posed. To look for *the author* of an oral epic is to look for an individual where a collective technique is at work, refined over generations of singers before being fixed one day by writing. “Homer” perhaps designates less a person than a tradition that had reached its end.

The shift goes beyond ancient Greece. Every culture that passed down long narratives before writing had to solve the same practical problem: how to hold thousands of lines in memory, in performance, without a safety net? The answer, found independently each time, resembles that of Međedović, one evening in July, in a small town in Montenegro.

repere.texte: Between July 5 and 12, 1935, in Bijelo Polje, the singer Avdo Međedović dictates to Parry and Lord a poem of 12,311 lines, without ever having written it, or even memorized it in the sense in which that is usually understood.

carte.punch: In 1935, an illiterate farmer recites 12,311 lines from memory, and changes how Homer is read.
carte.idee: The Homeric question asks who composed the Iliad and the Odyssey. Milman Parry answers it by recording illiterate singers in the Balkans who improvise thousands of lines using ready-made formulas, the same as Homer's.
carte.source_courte: M. Parry, Harvard Studies in Classical Philology, 1930

pour_aller_plus_loin.titre: Milman Parry Collection of Oral Literature — Harvard University
pour_aller_plus_loin.note: The archive collection: discs, notebooks, and transcriptions from the Yugoslav fieldwork of 1933-1935.

quiz.question: Why does the density of repeated formulas in Homer interest researchers who study oral composition?
choix: Because it proves that Homer mastered writing better than his contemporaries
Because it indicates that scribes corrupted the text over successive copies
Because such a density of formulas is the signature of improvisation in performance, not of unhurried writing
Because it demonstrates that the Iliad and the Odyssey must have been composed by the same person
quiz.explication: A poet who writes can reread himself and vary his vocabulary; a bard who improvises live needs fixed blocks to keep the rhythm going while he invents what comes next. The density of formulas says nothing about Homer's identity, or about the fidelity of the copies: it signals a technique of composition, found identically among illiterate singers in the Balkans in the 20th century.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When and where does Milman Parry go to Yugoslavia alone for a first scouting trip, before returning with Albert Lord?
choix: In 1930, to Belgrade, just after the publication of his study at Harvard
In the summer of 1933, scouting, before returning from June 1934 to September 1935 with Lord
In 1935, only a few weeks before the recording of Međedović
In 1928, two years before the publication of his hypothesis on formulas
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Parry first goes to Yugoslavia in the summer of 1933, alone, on a scouting trip, before returning from June 1934 to September 1935, this time with Albert Lord.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What stylistic problem in the Iliad and the Odyssey does the Homeric question raise, according to the entry?
choix: The abundance of fixed epithets, repeated without varying even when they fit the scene poorly
The use of two different Greek dialects depending on the books of the poem
The total absence of any mention of the gods in certain passages
The presence of technological anachronisms spotted by archaeologists
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The abundance of fixed epithets such as swift-footed Achilles, repeated without varying even when they do not fit the scene, is what has intrigued philologists since antiquity.

quiz_supplementaire.question: How does Parry and Lord's discovery shift the question of Homer's identity, rather than answer it?
choix: It proves that the Iliad and the Odyssey were written by two different authors
It demonstrates that Homer never existed and that his name is a late invention
It places the composition of the two poems several centuries after the generally accepted date
It shows that a collective technique, refined over generations, can produce the work, not just an individual
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The conclusion names no author: it shows that a collective technique of oral composition, refined over generations of singers, can produce a work of this scale.
